name: Agent Negotiation in Over-the-Counter Markets
title: Agent Negotiation in Over-the-Counter Markets
answer: Agent Negotiation in Over-the-Counter Markets covers software agents that quote, counter-quote and agree terms for instruments traded bilaterally rather than on an exchange. The scope includes request-for-quote workflows, streaming prices, inventory and hedging constraints, and the credit and collateral terms that sit alongside price. It sits inside Agent Workflows in Finance, where the unit of work is a negotiation between two parties rather than a single order sent to a matching engine. The instruments in view are bonds, swaps, repos, foreign exchange and other contracts whose terms are agreed privately.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Agent Negotiation in Over-the-Counter Markets covers software agents that quote, counter-quote and agree terms for instruments traded bilaterally rather than on an exchange. The scope includes request-for-quote workflows, streaming prices, inventory and hedging constraints, and the credit and collateral terms that sit alongside price. It sits inside Agent Workflows in Finance, where the unit of work is a negotiation between two parties rather than a single order sent to a matching engine. The instruments in view are bonds, swaps, repos, foreign exchange and other contracts whose terms are agreed privately.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: These agents run on top of electronic trading venues, dealer platforms and internal pricing engines, with market data, reference data and counterparty records feeding the same loop. A typical stack pairs a quoting or pricing model with a policy layer that decides when to hold, improve or walk away, plus a messaging layer that speaks the venue's protocol. Latency budgets are looser than in listed markets because negotiation takes turns, so the harder constraint is consistency between the agent's quotes and the firm's live risk. Audit logging of every message and decision is part of the infrastructure, not an add-on.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is usually framed as a sequential game: each side observes the other's quotes and responds under its own limits. Practitioners combine rule-based quoting with learned policies trained in simulation, then constrain the output with hard bounds on price, size and exposure. Evaluation leans on replaying historical request-for-quote sessions and on counterfactual tests against recorded counterparty behaviour. Because counterparties adapt, a policy that looks strong in backtest can degrade once it is live, so teams monitor for shifts in how others respond.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Firms treat agent negotiation as a regulated activity, so conduct rules, best execution duties and market abuse controls apply to the messages an agent sends. Records must show who authorised a quote, what limits applied and why a trade was agreed, which puts pressure on explainability for learned policies. Counterparty onboarding, credit lines and collateral terms are checked before an agent can trade, and pre-trade risk checks sit in the path.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Expect more negotiation to move from chat and voice into structured agent-to-agent protocols, with standard schemas for quotes, terms and settlement instructions. That shift raises the value of interoperability and of shared ways to prove what an agent did and under whose authority. Smaller dealers may gain access to liquidity that was previously relationship-bound, while venues and regulators push for common audit formats. The open questions are how to keep learned policies inside conduct rules and how liability is split when two agents agree on terms a human would have questioned.
